ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: The image shows an ant at the lower left of a square grid. The square grid can be understood as a grid with 3 lattice points on each side, that is, a 3×3 lattice-point array with coordinates from (0,0) to (2,2). Now model according to the problem statement and the specified method: the ant goes from the lower-left corner (0,0) to the upper-right corner (2,2), and can only move up, right, and left, not down. Because it cannot move down, to go from the bottom row to the top row it must and only needs to move up twice: once from the bottom row to the middle row, and once from the middle row to the top row. The first upward move can be chosen to occur in any one of columns 0, 1, and 2, for a total of 3 choices. The second upward move can also be chosen to occur in any one of columns 0, 1, and 2, for a total of 3 choices. On each row, when moving horizontally from one column position to another column position, if the same edge cannot be traversed repeatedly, the horizontal route is unique: either go directly left/right to the target column, or stay in place. Therefore the total number of paths is 3×3=9.

raw_record.question_text: An ant is standing at the bottom left corner of a 3 by 3 grid. How many ways can it get to the top right corner if it can only move up, right, and left, and it is not allowed to cross the same edge twice?

method.method_draft: Model the pictured grid as a 3-by-3 array of lattice points, with bottom-left at coordinate (0,0) and top-right at (2,2). Since the ant cannot move down, any valid path must use exactly two upward moves: one from the bottom row to the middle row and one from the middle row to the top row. Between upward moves, it may move horizontally along a row. On a row with three vertices, from any starting column to any ending column there is exactly one possible horizontal trail that does not repeat an edge: go directly along the row, or stay put. Thus choose the column of the first upward move in 3 ways and the column of the second upward move in 3 ways, giving 3 × 3 = 9 paths.

method.method_draft: Use a row-by-row dynamic programming transition table. Label the possible column positions on each row as 0, 1, and 2. For one horizontal row segment, define T(a,b) as the number of ways to move from column a to column b without repeating a horizontal edge before moving up. Because the row is just a 3-vertex line, T(a,b)=1 for every pair a,b: either stay still or move straight along the needed edges. Starting at column 0 on the bottom row, sum over all possible middle-row entry columns and top-row entry columns: T(0,i) · T(i,j) · T(j,2) for i,j in {0,1,2}. Since every factor is 1, there are 9 total paths.
